# Native growing quadratic-tower squareclasses: one bounded proof attack
Current state: compact sparse wave full spatial sampling classically matched; line parked. The next externally motivated question is complete squareclass and Selmer arithmetic in growing quadratic towers. Prior general-number-field quantum compact isotropy and Selmer endpoints under explicit GRH are already written in this repo; another quantum conic claim is not new.

Input tower Q=F0 subset F1 subset ... subset Fh, Fi=F(i-1)(sqrt(di)), with all field/basis embeddings and maximal-order multiplication tables explicitly supplied and charged; total degree N=2^h, total input bit length B. S_Q is explicit rational primes containing 2 and every tower ramification prime; S_i contains every Fi-prime above it. Target complete basis of Fh(S_h,2) with expanded polynomial-bit representatives (or a clearly separated compact variant with a paid support/factorization interface), bounded-error poly(N,B,log1/eta) time with integer factorization of polynomial-bit intermediates explicitly charged. No class group, units, norm witnesses, principal ideals or auxiliary prime supplied. A successful classical factoring reduction would match a quantum factoring composition for this family, not prove classical hardness or a speedup beyond factoring. Unconditional is preferred; state exact GRH dependencies if needed.

Candidate mechanism: Hilbert-symbol norm subspaces + Kutas quadratic-extension conic descent + support-obstruction quotient kernel. Let L=F(sqrt d), S include2/ramification. Compute V=F(S,2) intersect N(L*). For each basis a_i find beta_i with N beta_i=a_i c_i^2. Factor all numerator AND denominator norms to find E of outside-S F-prime support. Their outside-S parity vectors J_i pull back from F (equal split parities; inert parity also counts). Compute complete F(S union E,2) and its parity image W in F2^E. Then the true norm image of L(S_L,2) is C=kernel(c maps to sum c_i J_i mod W); correct beta-products with an element of F(S union E,2) solving the parity equation. Append F(S,2)/<d>. This removes the old odd-S-class promise at fixed quartic degree. Completeness uses (x+c)^2=(Tr x+2c)x when N x=c^2, with scalar exception handled. It is an algebraic mechanism, not yet a uniform tower clock.

Known blockers: Kutas Remark22 reduces ternary isotropy over a quadratic extension to 3,4,6-variable isotropy over the base. A ternary-only induction is circular. Koprowski Algorithm1 for quaternary forms needs complete base squareclasses, auxiliary-prime enlargement and two ternary norm solves. Its AppendixA inverse product of prime norms is NOT polynomial in bit length; a weak bound is not a runtime lower bound. Polynomial-per-level with degree-dependent branching or support growth can yield N^{O(log N)} or worse. Expanded conic output heights must be charged; compact circuits alone cannot be norm-factored in poly time.

Prior work checks: corpus been-tried and baselines run Nov13 for exact tower/conic/support question, returned noisy unrelated records plus LLL; targeted notes read. Primary Kutas1606.01053v2 and Koprowski2111.08569v2 actual algorithms/Remark22/AppendixA read, source excerpts attached. Existing fixed quadratic and promised quartic factoring baselines already proved; generic class/S-unit computation remains strongest general classical comparator under its actual conditions. No quantum implementation selected. Deliver one decisive theorem, explicit counterexample, or exact remaining gate, with all quantifiers and representations. Avoid lists of speculative repairs. Passing examples and report labels never prove an algorithm.

                   Appendix A. Complexity of Algorithm 1
   A detailed complexity analysis of algorithms presented in this paper seems to
be very diﬃcult, and deﬁnitely exceeds the competence of the author. One of the
reasons is that to the best of our knowledge not all of the external subroutines, we
rely on, oﬀer such a rigorous complexity analysis. In this appendix we provide a
crude estimate for the time complexity of Algorithm 1.
   Let K be a global ﬁeld represented either in the form K = Q(θ), if K is a
number ﬁeld, or K = Fpk (x, θ), if it is a function ﬁeld. Denote the monic minimal
polynomial of θ by f and let d be the degree of f . An element of K can be expressed
as a linear combination of successive powers of θ, say a = a0 + a1 θ + · · · + ad−1θd−1 .
Deﬁne the size of a to be the sum of bit-sizes of a0 , . . . , ad−1 . For a quadratic form q
over K, deﬁne its size as a sum of sizes of its coeﬃcients.
   In order to construct the set P(q) in step (2) of the algorithm, one has to factor
the principal ideals generated by K-integral representatives of square classes of
coeﬃcients of q. If K is a number ﬁeld, this problem can be reduced in polynomial
time to the problem of factoring integers (see, e.g., [11, §2.3.5]). The best known
algorithms for the latter task are sub-exponential in size of the input. GNFS (see,
e.g., [6], [26]) has complexity
                      √         Ln (1/3, (64/9)1/3 ), while ECM (see, e.g., [29], [19]) has
complexity Lp (1/2, 2), where p is the smallest prime dividing the integer to be
factored. Now, the computation of a norm increases the size of the input by the
factor |K : Q| and so the complexity of step (2) for number ﬁelds is sub-exponential
in the size of the form and the degree of the ﬁeld.
   If K is a global function ﬁeld, a ﬁnite extension of Fpk (x), then the problem
of factoring the ideals can be analogously reduced to factoring polynomials over
a ﬁnite ﬁeld. The later problem is well-known to be polynomial-time in the size
of the input (see, e.g., [43, Section 14.8]) Hence, for function ﬁelds step (2) has
polynomial time in size of the input and the degree d.
   Now, steps (3–4) are meaningful only for formally real ﬁelds (hence, necessarily
number ﬁelds). They boil down to performing a real root isolation of polynomials
with rational coeﬃcients. This can be done in polynomial time with respect to the
degree |K : Q| and the logarithm of the root distance. For details we refer the
reader to [1, Section 10.2] (see also [2, Section 3]).
   As expected, it is the analysis of the loop in step (5) which is most involving.
The construction in step (5a) of the basis B from scratch during the ﬁrst execution
of the loop can be reduced in polynomial time (with respect to the size of S)
to the problem of computing the S-unit group. For a general number ﬁeld, the
author is not aware of any algorithm for a latter task that would oﬀer a complexity
better than exponential in the size of S and the bit-size of the discriminant of K.
Related sub-exponential algorithms (see, e.g., [3]) rely on some heuristics. On the
other hand, as explained in Remark 1, in subsequent iterations of the loop, after
expanding S, the basis B can be updated incrementally in time polynomial with
respect to the size of S and the class number of K. The corresponding algorithm for
function ﬁelds is described in [21]. It is likely that one can use a similar incremental
algorithm also for number ﬁelds. However, to the best of our knowledge no such
algorithm has ever been published.
